tagline: From Salvador's seven-million-passenger bay to the Costa Verde islands and the ferry crossings of the industrial south — Brazil's coast already moves on the water, on slow diesel boats waiting to fly.
summary: Brazil's seaboard is not one market but a string of them, and in city after city the fastest line between two points is across the water. Salvador sits on Baía de Todos os Santos, Brazil's largest bay, where a state-regulated ferry-and-lancha habit already carries millions of passengers a year. Rio de Janeiro, a coastal megacity, sits an hour's water from the Costa Verde — Angra dos Reis, Ilha Grande and a labyrinth of islands. Along the São Paulo coast, São Sebastião faces the sailing-capital island of Ilhabela across a channel where cars queue for hours, and Santos and Guarujá are split by 400 metres of water that carry tens of thousands of people a day. Vitória has already proved urban water transit works, and to the south Florianópolis anchors a marina belt while Ilha do Mel is a car-free island reachable only by boat. Today these crossings run on slow ferries, schooners and diesel launches. A clean, fast, stabilised foiling tier is the premium-but-practical layer Brazil's coast has never had.
why_marine_mobility: Brazil's coastal story repeats from the northeast to the south: a bay or a channel where the water route is short and the road route is long, slow and congested. From Salvador's Terminal Náutico across Baía de Todos os Santos to Morro de São Paulo; from Rio's marinas to Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande; across the São Sebastião channel to Ilhabela; over the mouth of the Port of Santos to Guarujá; across the Baía de Vitória under the Terceira Ponte; and out to car-free Ilha do Mel — every one of these is a trip better made on the water. Navier's Pioneer II foiling tier turns those crossings into smooth, dry, on-demand legs, while the same craft serves the dense marina-to-marina hops around the Costa Verde and Florianópolis — essential coastal commuting and premium leisure on one clean platform.

demand_signals.label: Salvador — a bay that already moves millions
demand_signals.note: Baía de Todos os Santos, Brazil's largest bay, carries around 7.5 million passengers a year on a state-regulated (AGERBA) ferry-and-lancha network serving a 2.9-million-person metro.

demand_signals.label: Santos–Guarujá — the world's busiest little crossing
demand_signals.note: The 400-metre harbour-mouth crossing at Latin America's largest port moves more than 36,000 people and vehicles a day; the alternative by road is a 45 km detour. A state contract now mandates an electric fleet.

demand_signals.label: Vitória — urban water transit, already proven
demand_signals.note: The relaunched Baía de Vitória ferry carried over 1.2 million riders in under three years, and the state is building three more stations — demand for clean bay transit is already demonstrated.

demand_signals.label: Ilhabela — a three-minute crossing behind a four-hour queue
demand_signals.note: Brazil's sailing capital (about 1.5 million visitors a year) sits barely 1.3 nm off the mainland, yet cars queue four-plus hours for the diesel ferry and 5,700 pedestrians a day cross the only 24-hour link.

demand_signals.label: Ilha do Mel — a car-free island reachable only by boat
demand_signals.note: Paraná's most-visited state park drew 247,020 visitors in 2025, every one arriving by a state-regulated boat crossing — a captive, clean-transit-ready corridor.

demand_signals.label: Costa Verde leisure density
demand_signals.note: Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande — a 365-island archipelago of beaches, marinas and resorts — draw heavy yacht, charter and day-trip traffic from Rio's affluent market.

demand_signals.label: Florianópolis marina belt
demand_signals.note: Florianópolis and Santa Catarina concentrate a dense cluster of marinas and island beaches with an established boating culture and high domestic-tourism volume.

use_cases.body: Regulated bay and channel commutes — Salvador's São Joaquim–Bom Despacho and Mar Grande lines, the Santos–Guarujá harbour crossing, and the Baía de Vitória run — flown clean, fast and on-demand in place of slow diesel ferries.

Island resort and day-trip transfers — Salvador to Morro de São Paulo, São Sebastião to Ilhabela, and Pontal do Sul to car-free Ilha do Mel — smooth, dry crossings that replace long ferry queues and open-swell schooner runs.

Costa Verde and marina leisure — Rio's affluent market to Angra dos Reis and Ilha Grande, plus the dense marina-to-marina hops around Angra and Florianópolis — a premium water product the coast has never had.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Almost the entire network sits inside Pioneer II's 70-nautical-mile range at 30 knots: Salvador's bay crossings and the ~34 nm Morro de São Paulo run, the Rio–Costa Verde corridor and Angra marina hops, the ~1.3 nm São Sebastião–Ilhabela channel, the Santos–Guarujá harbour mouth, the Baía de Vitória, and the Ilha do Mel and Florianópolis legs — all commercial-ready today.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Longer coastal trunks — linking clusters up and down the seaboard, or the ~700 nm-class line-haul legs no day-boat can serve — are Quanta-LR corridors (hybrid range, H2 2026+).

signature_routes.label: Costa Verde headline — Angra dos Reis ↔ Ilha Grande
Costa Verde marina hop — Marina Bracuhy ↔ Marina Cacolaco (Angra)
Salvador flagship — Terminal Náutico ↔ Morro de São Paulo (~34 nm)
São Sebastião ↔ Ilhabela (Barra Velha) — the 24-hour channel lifeline
Santos ↔ Guarujá — the 400 m harbour-mouth crossing
Vitória — Prainha ↔ Praça do Papa, under the Terceira Ponte
Ilha do Mel — Pontal do Sul ↔ Nova Brasília (the only way in)

transit_planning: For a marina group, resort operator or regional tourism authority: a clean, fast, on-demand water tier that connects Rio's affluent market to the Costa Verde and stitches together the fragmented Angra and Florianópolis marina belts. Start with the proven short Costa Verde and Florianópolis hops on Pioneer II — riding existing berths and jetties with no new infrastructure — then extend to longer coastal trunks on Quanta-LR as range comes online.
competitive_landscape: Across every one of these cities the water runs on the same three options: conventional ferries and state-regulated lanchas (cheap but slow and fixed-schedule), schooner and day-trip boats (scenic but unhurried), and private launches (fast but diesel and costly). There is no clean, on-demand premium tier. Navier's foiling craft is the missing option — faster and smoother than a ferry, cleaner and quieter than a diesel launch — and in several markets (Santos, Salvador, Ilha do Mel) the crossing is already regulated and, at Santos, an electric fleet is now mandated.
regulatory_note: Brazilian maritime passenger transport is overseen by the Marinha do Brasil (Navy) port-captaincy system and ANTAQ (the national waterway transport agency), with state agencies regulating local crossings — AGERBA in Bahia (Salvador), the DER/State of São Paulo contract for Santos–Guarujá, and Paraná's authority for Ilha do Mel. Passenger operation requires vessel registration and crew certification under the Tribunal Marítimo framework; state and municipal transport and tourism authorities are the natural first touchpoints.
seasonality: The Brazilian summer (Dec–Mar) brings peak leisure demand and the calmest, warmest conditions coast-wide; the southern winter (Jun–Aug) is cooler with more frontal weather pushing up from the south, and the northeast (Salvador) has its wettest months around Apr–Jul. A stabilised foiling craft holds comfort and schedule in the shoulder and open-swell windows — such as Salvador's open-Atlantic run to Morro de São Paulo — where conventional craft get rough.

precedents.what: Four Seasons Lake Austin operates an N30 in live luxury-hospitality service — proof of the premium water-shuttle model Navier brings to Brazil's coastal and island corridors.
